roadmaps.tagline: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Cognizant, Capgemini
roadmaps.summary: The shortest honest path to clearing a mass-recruiter drive. These companies test breadth, not depth: clean basics, steady coding, aptitude, and the confidence to explain what you wrote. Work through this in order and you will have seen every shape of question they ask.
roadmaps.forWho: Pre-final and final year students sitting for campus drives.

nodes.title: Write and run programs without hesitating
nodes.why: Every drive starts with a timed online round. Fumbling over input parsing or a for-loop costs you the questions you could have solved.

nodes.title: Arrays
nodes.why: More campus coding questions are array questions than anything else: traversal, searching, rotation, sub-arrays.

nodes.title: Strings
nodes.why: Palindromes, anagrams, reversal, counting characters. Cheap marks once you stop fearing index arithmetic.

nodes.title: Searching and sorting
nodes.why: Binary search turns a brute-force timeout into a pass. Knowing which sort to reach for is routinely asked aloud in interviews.

nodes.title: Hashing
nodes.why: The single highest-leverage idea in this list: it collapses most nested-loop solutions into one pass.

nodes.title: Two pointers and sliding window
nodes.why: The two patterns that come up whenever a question says subarray, pair, or without repeating characters.

nodes.title: Stacks, queues and linked lists
nodes.why: Rarely the hard question, often the viva question. You are expected to be able to draw one and code one.

nodes.title: Recursion and introductory DP
nodes.why: Fibonacci, staircase, coin change. Service companies stop about here, so a working memoised solution is enough.

nodes.title: Aptitude and logical reasoning
nodes.why: The round most people lose, because they practise code and assume aptitude will take care of itself. It will not: it is timed arithmetic under pressure.

nodes.title: Company-pattern practice
nodes.why: Each recruiter has habits. Sit the company sets closest to your drive once you can already solve the topics above.

nodes.title: Explain your own code out loud
nodes.why: The technical interview is mostly walk me through what you did. Re-open three problems you solved and narrate the approach, the complexity, and one case you got wrong first.

roadmaps.tagline: Core Java, collections, Spring Boot
roadmaps.summary: Java is still what most Indian service and product companies build on. This path takes you from syntax to a deployable Spring Boot service, with the data-structure work that interviews actually test sitting alongside it rather than after it.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting Java backend roles, or anyone whose college stack is Java.

nodes.title: Java syntax and your first programs
nodes.why: Types, loops, methods, and reading input. Nothing here is interesting, and everything later depends on it.

nodes.title: Arrays and strings
nodes.why: A Java String is immutable and a Java array is fixed-length. Both facts shape how you solve almost every question.

nodes.title: Object-oriented programming
nodes.why: Classes, inheritance, interfaces, polymorphism. This is the part of the interview where a wrong answer is remembered.

nodes.text: Already know OOP from C++ or Python? Skim this one — the concepts transfer, only the keywords change.

nodes.title: Collections framework
nodes.why: List, Set, Map, and when each one is the right answer. Being able to describe HashMap is close to mandatory.

nodes.title: Exceptions and file I/O
nodes.why: Checked versus unchecked, try-with-resources, and reading a file without leaking a handle.

nodes.title: Linked lists, stacks and queues
nodes.why: Implement them once by hand. After that you will understand what the library is doing for you.

nodes.title: Trees and graphs
nodes.why: Traversals, depth, and the two searches. Where product-company interviews start and service-company ones usually stop.

nodes.title: Dynamic programming
nodes.why: Recognising overlapping subproblems. Aim for a correct memo table before you chase elegance.

nodes.title: SQL and databases
nodes.why: Every backend role asks for joins, grouping and an index. It is the most reliably examined non-Java topic in a Java interview.

nodes.title: Spring Boot and REST APIs
nodes.why: Controllers, dependency injection, and a service that answers on a port. This is what the job is.

reading.label: Spring: Building a RESTful Web Service

nodes.title: Ship one project, then prepare to defend it
nodes.why: A small, finished, deployed service beats three half-built ones. Be ready to explain every dependency you added.

roadmaps.tagline: Python, SQL, pandas, statistics
roadmaps.summary: Analyst roles reward a different skill from software roles: getting a messy table into a shape that answers a question, and then saying what it means. Python and SQL are the tools; the judgement is the job.
roadmaps.forWho: Students aiming at data analyst, BI or junior data science roles.

nodes.title: Python basics
nodes.why: Loops, functions, conditionals, input. Get fluent enough that the language stops being the obstacle.

nodes.title: Lists, dictionaries and sets
nodes.why: Almost all data cleaning is dictionary work in disguise. Counting and grouping by hand first will make pandas make sense later.

nodes.title: Strings and text handling
nodes.why: Real data arrives dirty: trailing spaces, mixed case, inconsistent separators. Text wrangling is most of the work.

nodes.title: Sorting, searching and slicing
nodes.why: Top-N, ranking and lookups are the questions analysts are actually asked, every week.

nodes.title: Recursion and problem decomposition
nodes.why: Less for the interview than for the habit: break a question into a smaller version of itself before writing anything.

nodes.title: NumPy and pandas
nodes.why: DataFrames, filtering, groupby, merge. The point where you stop writing loops over rows.

nodes.title: SQL for analysis
nodes.why: This is the round you will be tested on. Joins, GROUP BY, then window functions, in that order.

nodes.title: Statistics you will be asked about
nodes.why: Mean versus median and why it matters, distributions, correlation is not causation, and what a p-value does and does not say.

nodes.title: Visualisation and explaining a result
nodes.why: A chart that needs explaining has failed. Practise reducing a finding to one sentence and one picture.

nodes.title: One end-to-end analysis
nodes.why: Take a public dataset, ask a real question, clean it, chart it, and write the answer in a paragraph. That is your portfolio.

roadmaps.tagline: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Node — the full-stack path
roadmaps.summary: The fastest route to something you can show someone. You build visible things early, which keeps motivation up, but the fundamentals still decide whether you pass the interview, so they stay in the path rather than being skipped.
roadmaps.forWho: Students aiming at frontend, full-stack or product-engineering roles.

nodes.title: Programming foundations
nodes.why: Frameworks change every two years. Loops, functions and conditionals do not.

nodes.title: HTML and CSS
nodes.why: Semantic markup, the box model, flexbox and grid. Most of the frustration here is one unread page of documentation.

nodes.title: JavaScript fundamentals
nodes.why: Arrays and strings are where JavaScript is actually written: map, filter, reduce, split, join.

nodes.title: The DOM and browser APIs
nodes.why: Events, fetch, and local storage. Enough to make a page respond to a person without any framework at all.

nodes.title: Data structures behind the UI
nodes.why: Hash maps for lookups, stacks for undo and history. Interviews ask these even for frontend roles.

nodes.title: Git and the command line
nodes.why: Branch, commit, merge, resolve a conflict. Not optional, and quietly assessed from your first day.

nodes.title: React
nodes.why: Components, state and props. Learn why re-renders happen before learning the hooks that work around them.

nodes.title: Node and REST APIs
nodes.why: A server, a route, a JSON response. Once your own frontend talks to your own backend, full-stack stops being a buzzword.

nodes.title: Databases
nodes.why: Store something that survives a restart. Schemas, queries, and why you never concatenate user input into SQL.

nodes.title: Algorithms for the interview round
nodes.why: Even frontend interviews include one coding question. Two pointers, searching and a little recursion cover most of them.

nodes.title: Deploy it, then write about it
nodes.why: A live URL and a readable README are worth more than a private repository with twice the code.

roadmaps.tagline: Amazon, Flipkart, product startups — harder DSA, a design round
roadmaps.summary: The step up from a mass-recruiter drive: fewer, harder DSA rounds, a lightweight system-design question even at the SDE-1 level, and a behavioural round that actually gets read. This path assumes you can already write working code and focuses on what separates a pass from a reject at this tier.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting product companies and well-funded startups, after or alongside Service-Company Placement.

nodes.title: Fundamentals, at interview speed
nodes.why: A product company's online round assumes basics are already fast, not a learning step — time pressure is the actual test here.

nodes.title: Arrays and strings, under time pressure
nodes.why: The first filter round is almost always an array or string question with a strict time limit.

nodes.title: Hashing and frequency problems
nodes.why: The fastest way to turn an O(n²) brute force into O(n) — the single highest-leverage pattern in these interviews.

nodes.title: Two pointers and sliding window
nodes.why: Comes up whenever a question mentions subarray, pair, or window — recognise the pattern and the solution writes itself.

nodes.title: Binary search, including on the answer
nodes.why: Past the obvious sorted-array case, product companies test binary-search-on-the-answer — a different skill from the textbook version.

nodes.title: Trees and graphs, properly
nodes.why: BFS and DFS are assumed knowledge here, not the finish line — expect a traversal plus a twist.

nodes.title: Dynamic programming, the real kind
nodes.why: 2D DP and DP-on-trees separate this tier from a mass-recruiter drive. Aim for a correct state transition before optimising space.

nodes.title: System design basics
nodes.why: Even an SDE-1 round at a product company asks one lightweight design question — you are not expected to design Netflix, just to reason about trade-offs out loud.

nodes.title: The behavioural round
nodes.why: This round is scored as rigorously as the coding one at most product companies — a vague answer here fails a candidate who cleared every DSA round.

nodes.title: Run timed mock interviews before the real one
nodes.why: The clock and a stranger watching you think changes everything. Simulate it before it happens for real.

roadmaps.tagline: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React — the narrower, faster path
roadmaps.summary: Everything a frontend role actually tests, without the backend and database detour the full-stack path includes. For a student who already knows this is the direction and wants to get there faster.
roadmaps.forWho: Students specifically targeting frontend or UI-engineering roles, not full-stack.

nodes.title: Programming foundations
nodes.why: Frameworks change every two years. Loops, functions and conditionals do not.

nodes.title: HTML and CSS
nodes.why: Semantic markup, the box model, flexbox and grid — most frustration here is one unread page of documentation.

nodes.title: JavaScript fundamentals
nodes.why: Arrays and strings are where JavaScript is actually written: map, filter, reduce, split, join.

nodes.title: The DOM and browser APIs
nodes.why: Events, fetch, local storage — enough to make a page respond to a person without any framework at all.

nodes.title: Data structures behind the UI
nodes.why: Hash maps for lookups, stacks for undo and history — interviews ask these even for frontend roles.

nodes.title: React
nodes.why: Components, state and props — learn why re-renders happen before learning the hooks that work around them.

nodes.title: Routing and forms
nodes.why: A real app has more than one screen and takes input. Both are where most beginner React projects first break.

nodes.title: Build tooling and package managers
nodes.why: Vite, npm, and why `node_modules` exists — invisible until the day it breaks your build.

nodes.title: Git and the command line
nodes.why: Branch, commit, merge, resolve a conflict — not optional, and quietly assessed from your first day.

nodes.title: Deploy it, then write about it
nodes.why: A live URL and a readable README are worth more than a private repository with twice the code.

roadmaps.tagline: JavaScript/TypeScript, Express, REST APIs, databases
roadmaps.summary: The JavaScript-stack counterpart to the Java Developer path. For students who already know JS from frontend work, or prefer one language across the stack.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting backend or full-stack roles on a JavaScript/TypeScript stack.

nodes.title: JavaScript fundamentals
nodes.why: Closures, async/await, and the event loop — the parts of JS that backend work actually exercises.

nodes.title: Arrays and strings
nodes.why: The data every API request and response is built from, one way or another.

nodes.title: Hashing and maps
nodes.why: Caching, deduplication, and lookup tables — used constantly in real backend code, not just interviews.

nodes.title: Trees, graphs and dynamic programming
nodes.why: Less common day-to-day, but still the interview filter for this role at most companies.

nodes.title: Node.js and Express
nodes.why: A server, a route, a JSON response — the actual job, once you can write one.

nodes.title: REST API design
nodes.why: Resource naming, status codes, and versioning — the difference between an API other teams can use and one they complain about.

nodes.title: Databases and ORMs
nodes.why: Schemas, queries, and why you never concatenate user input into SQL.

nodes.title: Authentication and security basics
nodes.why: Hashing passwords, issuing tokens, and the handful of mistakes that account for most real breaches.

nodes.title: Testing and Git
nodes.why: A backend without tests breaks silently. Branch, commit, merge — not optional here either.

nodes.title: Deploy a working API, then explain it
nodes.why: A deployed service with three well-tested endpoints beats five half-built ones.

roadmaps.tagline: Kotlin, Android SDK — DSA tracked, Android-specific nodes are reading
roadmaps.summary: Kotlin and the Android SDK have no code-judge here, so those nodes are reading and checkpoints rather than tracked practice. The DSA spine underneath is identical to every other role, because the interview filter is too.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting Android roles. Reading-heavy: the DSA nodes are tracked, the Android-specific ones are not.

nodes.title: Kotlin fundamentals
nodes.why: Kotlin is the modern Android language — null safety and data classes are where it most differs from Java.

nodes.title: Arrays and strings
nodes.why: Same interview filter every other role faces first, language aside.

nodes.title: Hashing, stacks and queues
nodes.why: The standard-library structures every Android app's business logic quietly relies on.

nodes.title: Trees, graphs and dynamic programming
nodes.why: Less directly relevant to app code, but still asked in the same interview as the Android-specific questions.

nodes.title: Activities, Fragments and the lifecycle
nodes.why: The single most-asked conceptual Android question: what happens to your screen on rotation, and why.

nodes.title: Jetpack Compose
nodes.why: Google's current recommended UI toolkit — declarative, and increasingly what interviews expect over the old View system.

nodes.title: Networking and local storage
nodes.why: Retrofit for the network call, Room for what survives after the app closes — most real apps need both.

reading.label: Android: Save data in a local database

nodes.title: App architecture
nodes.why: MVVM and a ViewModel that survives rotation — the difference between a demo app and a maintainable one.

nodes.title: Publish one app, then prepare to defend it
nodes.why: A real app on a real device, with a Play Store listing draft even if never actually published, beats a dozen tutorial clones.

roadmaps.tagline: Python, statistics, scikit-learn, model evaluation
roadmaps.summary: Builds on the same Python foundation Python / Data Analyst uses, then goes further into actual model training and evaluation — the next step for a student who has already done the analyst path and wants the ML-engineering side.
roadmaps.forWho: Students aiming at data scientist, ML engineer, or applied-ML roles, ideally after or alongside Python / Data Analyst.

nodes.title: Python and NumPy/pandas
nodes.why: Vectorised operations over DataFrames — the baseline every ML library is built on top of.

nodes.title: Arrays, strings and hashing
nodes.why: The same interview filter every role faces, in Python this time.

nodes.title: Sorting, searching and recursion
nodes.why: Top-N and ranking questions are common in both the DSA round and the actual job.

nodes.title: Statistics for ML
nodes.why: Bias-variance, distributions, and what a p-value does and does not say — the theory every model-evaluation question assumes.

nodes.title: scikit-learn and model training
nodes.why: Fit, predict, score — the three calls almost every classical ML workflow comes down to.

nodes.title: Model evaluation
nodes.why: Accuracy lies on imbalanced data. Precision, recall and the confusion matrix are what interviewers actually probe.

nodes.title: Neural network basics
nodes.why: Not expected to train one from scratch at interview level, but expected to explain what a layer and a gradient actually do.

nodes.title: One end-to-end project, then defend it
nodes.why: A clean notebook with a real dataset, a trained model, and an honestly-reported accuracy is worth more than five tutorial copies.

roadmaps.tagline: Linux, Docker, CI/CD, cloud basics — reading-heavy
roadmaps.summary: None of this is code-judged here, so the whole path is reading and checkpoints rather than tracked practice. The value is a clear order to learn it in, not a progress bar.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting DevOps, SRE or platform-engineering roles. Fully reading-heavy: no tracked nodes on this platform today.

nodes.title: Linux fundamentals
nodes.why: Every production server a DevOps engineer touches is Linux. The shell is not optional background knowledge here.

nodes.title: Shell scripting
nodes.why: Automating a repeated task is the job description in one sentence.

nodes.title: Networking basics
nodes.why: DNS, load balancers, and what actually happens between a request and a response — debugging without this is guessing.

nodes.title: Docker
nodes.why: "Works on my machine" stops being an excuse once the image is the unit of deployment.

nodes.title: Kubernetes basics
nodes.why: Not expected to run a cluster solo on day one, but expected to know what a pod, a deployment and a service actually are.

nodes.title: CI/CD pipelines
nodes.why: A pipeline that runs tests and deploys on merge is what separates a hobby project from a production workflow.

nodes.title: Infrastructure as Code
nodes.why: Clicking buttons in a cloud console does not scale or survive an audit. Terraform does both.

nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (AWS)
nodes.why: AWS is the most commonly asked-about cloud in Indian hiring. EC2, S3 and IAM cover most interview questions.

nodes.title: Monitoring and logging
nodes.why: If nobody is paged before the customer notices, the monitoring does not count.

nodes.title: Automate one real deployment, then explain it
nodes.why: A project with a Dockerfile, a CI pipeline, and a one-command deploy beats a resume line that says "familiar with DevOps tools."

roadmaps.tagline: Testing fundamentals, Selenium/Playwright, API testing
roadmaps.summary: Scripting nodes are tracked against the same catalog every other role uses; the testing-tool nodes are reading, since there is no automated-testing judge here. A realistic path for a student who likes breaking things more than building them.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting QA, SDET or test-automation roles.

nodes.title: Programming foundations
nodes.why: Automation is code. Loops, functions and conditionals are not optional for this role either.

nodes.title: Arrays, strings and data handling
nodes.why: Test data generation and assertion checks are array and string problems in disguise.

nodes.title: Testing fundamentals
nodes.why: Unit, integration, and end-to-end are different questions answered by different tests — conflating them wastes effort on both sides.

nodes.title: Manual testing and bug reporting
nodes.why: Before automating anything, a QA engineer is judged on how clearly they can describe what went wrong and how to reproduce it.

reading.label: A Guide to Writing Bug Reports

nodes.title: Selenium / Playwright basics
nodes.why: Browser automation is the core SDET skill — finding an element and clicking it reliably is harder than it sounds.

nodes.title: API testing
nodes.why: Faster and more stable than UI tests, and most bugs are caught here before they ever reach the browser.

nodes.title: CI integration for test suites
nodes.why: A test suite nobody runs automatically on every change is a test suite that quietly goes stale.

nodes.title: Build one automated test suite, then defend it
nodes.why: A small, real test suite against a real app — explain what it catches and what it deliberately does not.

roadmaps.tagline: Pure problem-solving, any branch, any target role
roadmaps.summary: Language-agnostic, role-agnostic — the "I don't know what role yet, just make me interview-ready" option. Every pattern that shows up across every other roadmap's DSA sections, in one deliberately ordered path, taken further than any single role-roadmap goes.
roadmaps.forWho: Any student who wants deep DSA practice independent of a specific target role.

nodes.title: Arrays and strings
nodes.why: The most common question shape in any interview, in any company tier.

nodes.title: Searching and sorting
nodes.why: Binary search turns a brute-force timeout into a pass. Know which sort to reach for, and why.

nodes.title: Two pointers and sliding window
nodes.why: The two patterns behind most subarray and pair questions.

nodes.title: Linked lists, stacks and queues
nodes.why: Implement each one by hand once. After that you understand what the standard library is doing for you.

nodes.title: Hashing
nodes.why: The single highest-leverage idea on this list: it collapses most nested-loop solutions into one pass.

nodes.title: Trees
nodes.why: Traversals and depth first — most interviews start and a large share stop here.

nodes.title: Graphs
nodes.why: BFS, DFS, and the two searches cover most graph questions you will actually be asked.

nodes.title: Recursion and backtracking
nodes.why: Breaking a problem into a smaller version of itself — the habit behind most "hard" questions once you see it.

nodes.title: Dynamic programming
nodes.why: Recognising overlapping subproblems — aim for a correct memo table before you chase elegance.

nodes.title: Timed mock rounds
nodes.why: Solving a problem at your own pace and solving it in 25 minutes with someone watching are different skills. Practise the second one deliberately.

roadmaps.tagline: STL, time complexity, contest-style problem solving
roadmaps.summary: A distinct culture from mass-recruiter placement prep: contest ratings, the STL, and a faster, more ruthless kind of problem-solving. For the students already active on Codeforces or CodeChef, or who want to be.
roadmaps.forWho: Students interested in competitive programming specifically, usually alongside — not instead of — a placement-focused roadmap.

nodes.title: C++ syntax and fast I/O
nodes.why: `cin`/`cout` without sync is slow enough to time out a contest solution that is otherwise correct — the first lesson every competitive programmer learns the hard way.

nodes.title: Arrays, vectors and strings
nodes.why: `std::vector` and `std::string` are what you actually write in a contest, not raw arrays.

nodes.title: STL containers
nodes.why: `map`, `set`, `priority_queue` — knowing which container fits a problem shape is half the battle in a timed contest.

nodes.title: Time and space complexity under a strict limit
nodes.why: A 2-second time limit means roughly 10^8 operations — estimating this before you code saves a wasted submission.

nodes.title: Two pointers, sliding window and binary search
nodes.why: The three patterns that solve the majority of Div 2 A-C problems once recognised.

nodes.title: Graphs and trees
nodes.why: BFS, DFS, and basic shortest-path algorithms — the standard Div 2 D/E territory.

nodes.title: Dynamic programming
nodes.why: Where most contestants plateau — recognising the state and transition is a trained skill, not a flash of insight.

nodes.title: Rate yourself on Codeforces or CodeChef
nodes.why: A contest rating is an honest, external benchmark — virtual-participate in old contests to build the habit before rating is on the line.

roadmaps.tagline: SQL, schema design, indexing, transactions — reading-heavy
roadmaps.summary: No SQL judge on this platform yet, so every node here is reading and self-practice rather than tracked. Still the single most reliably-asked non-language-specific skill across every other technical interview.
roadmaps.forWho: Students who want to go deep on databases specifically, or need it as a weak area across other roadmaps. Fully reading-heavy: no tracked nodes on this platform today.

nodes.title: SELECT, WHERE and filtering
nodes.why: The query you write most often, and the one that is graded most strictly for correctness on edge cases.

nodes.title: Joins
nodes.why: The question asked in almost every analyst and backend interview — INNER vs LEFT is not a minor detail.

nodes.title: Aggregation and GROUP BY
nodes.why: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING — where most SQL interview questions actually live.

nodes.title: Subqueries and window functions
nodes.why: The question that separates "knows basic SQL" from "can actually write analytical queries."

nodes.title: Schema design and normalization
nodes.why: A well-normalized schema prevents entire categories of bugs before a line of application code is written.

nodes.title: Transactions and ACID
nodes.why: What actually happens if the power cuts mid-write — and why a banking app cannot afford to guess.

nodes.title: Indexing and query performance
nodes.why: An unindexed query that works fine on 100 rows can take down production at 10 million.

nodes.title: Write and explain 20 real queries
nodes.why: Pick a public dataset, write the queries a real analyst would be asked for, and be ready to explain why each one is correct and efficient.

roadmaps.tagline: AWS core services, IAM, networking — reading-heavy
roadmaps.summary: No cloud-console judge here, so this path is reading and the free-tier console itself, not tracked practice. Scoped to what actually gets asked in entry-level cloud interviews in India, not AWS's full certification syllabus.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting cloud/infrastructure roles, or preparing for AWS Cloud Practitioner / Solutions Architect Associate. Fully reading-heavy: no tracked nodes on this platform today.

nodes.title: What is cloud computing
nodes.why: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS, and why "the cloud" is just someone else's data center with an API — the mental model every other node builds on.

nodes.title: EC2 and compute
nodes.why: Launching and sizing a virtual machine correctly is the single most common first task in a cloud role.

nodes.title: S3 and storage
nodes.why: Object storage, not a file system — the distinction trips up almost everyone the first time.

nodes.title: RDS and managed databases
nodes.why: Running your own database server on a VM is almost never the right default once a managed option exists.

nodes.title: VPC and networking
nodes.why: Subnets, route tables and security groups — the layer every other AWS service sits inside.

nodes.title: IAM and security
nodes.why: The least-privilege principle, and the single most commonly misconfigured thing in real AWS incidents.

nodes.title: Serverless basics (Lambda)
nodes.why: Pay-per-execution, no server to patch — increasingly the first thing a small team reaches for.

nodes.title: Build one project on the AWS free tier
nodes.why: A static site on S3, an API on Lambda, or a VM running something real — the free tier is generous enough to actually build with, not just read about.

roadmaps.tagline: Networking, OWASP Top 10, basic pentesting — reading-heavy
roadmaps.summary: No exploit-grading judge here, so this is reading, labs on the student's own machine, and checkpoints rather than tracked practice. Scoped to the fundamentals that show up in both interviews and real incident reports, not a full red-team curriculum.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting security roles, or wanting security literacy alongside a development path. Fully reading-heavy: no tracked nodes on this platform today.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals
nodes.why: You cannot secure, or attack, what you don't understand at the packet level.

nodes.title: Linux for security work
nodes.why: Nearly every security tool assumes a Linux shell, usually Kali or Parrot OS.

nodes.title: OWASP Top 10
nodes.why: The single most commonly referenced list in both web security interviews and real incident write-ups.

nodes.title: Authentication and session security
nodes.why: Most real breaches are a credential or session problem, not a zero-day exploit.

nodes.title: Cryptography basics
nodes.why: Not expected to implement a cipher — expected to know why a known-broken one is still shipped in old code.

nodes.title: Reconnaissance and scanning
nodes.why: The first phase of any real penetration test, and the one most CTF challenges also start with.

nodes.title: Common vulnerabilities, hands-on
nodes.why: Reading about SQL injection and actually triggering one in a legal lab are different levels of understanding.

nodes.title: Complete a beginner CTF track, then write it up
nodes.why: TryHackMe or picoCTF's beginner paths, solved and documented — a concrete, verifiable claim beats "interested in security" on a resume.

roadmaps.tagline: Dart, Flutter widgets, one codebase for iOS and Android — reading-heavy
roadmaps.summary: No Flutter judge here, so this path is reading and the student's own emulator, not tracked practice. For a student who wants one app shipping to both app stores rather than choosing Android or iOS specifically.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting cross-platform mobile roles, or wanting one app on both stores without learning Kotlin and Swift separately. Fully reading-heavy: no tracked nodes on this platform today.

nodes.title: Dart fundamentals
nodes.why: Flutter is written in Dart — null safety and async/await look familiar from other languages, but Dart has its own rules worth learning properly first.

nodes.title: Widgets and layout
nodes.why: Everything in Flutter is a widget — understanding the tree is understanding the framework.

nodes.title: Navigation and routing
nodes.why: A real app has more than one screen — Navigator 2.0 is where most beginners first get stuck.

nodes.title: State management
nodes.why: setState works for a toy app and falls apart at real scale — knowing when to reach for Provider or Riverpod matters.

nodes.title: Networking and local storage
nodes.why: An API call and something that survives an app restart — most real apps need both from day one.

nodes.title: Platform-specific code
nodes.why: "Write once" is mostly true — knowing the handful of cases where it is not saves a debugging afternoon.

nodes.title: Testing in Flutter
nodes.why: Widget tests catch a broken layout before a user does, far cheaper than a one-star review.

nodes.title: Ship one app to both stores (or prepare to)
nodes.why: A real app, built and signed for both Android and iOS even if never actually published, is the concrete proof this path asks for.

roadmaps.tagline: Goroutines, channels, Go's standard library — reading-heavy
roadmaps.summary: Go is not enabled for submission on this platform yet, so the DSA nodes here route through a language you can actually submit — practise the algorithm in Python or Java, then apply it in Go yourself. The Go-specific nodes are reading.
roadmaps.forWho: Students specifically targeting Go roles (increasingly common in backend/infra hiring). DSA nodes route through another submittable language; Go-specific nodes are reading.

nodes.title: Go syntax and tooling
nodes.why: Go's syntax is deliberately small — most of it can be learned in a day, which is the language's whole design philosophy.

nodes.title: Arrays, slices and strings
nodes.why: This platform cannot judge Go submissions yet — practise the pattern in Python or Java here, then re-implement it in Go yourself to build the muscle memory.

nodes.title: Maps, hashing and structs
nodes.why: Same note as above: practise the algorithm in a submittable language, apply the pattern in Go's own map/struct syntax afterward.

nodes.title: Trees, graphs and dynamic programming
nodes.why: Same routing: the algorithm pattern transfers directly even though the submission happens in another language here.

nodes.title: Goroutines and channels
nodes.why: The reason teams pick Go for backend services — concurrency that is readable, not a tangle of callbacks.

nodes.title: The standard library
nodes.why: net/http and encoding/json cover most of what a Go backend service actually needs, with zero external dependencies.

nodes.title: Building a REST API in Go
nodes.why: A server, a route, a JSON response — the same job every backend role asks for, in Go's own idiom.

nodes.title: Ship one Go service, then defend it
nodes.why: A small, deployed Go API with goroutines actually doing something concurrent — not a hello-world handler.

roadmaps.tagline: Algorithms, complexity theory, core CS — for GATE or an MS application
roadmaps.summary: Mostly algorithms, complexity and core CS theory — genuinely DSA-trackable, and reuses the same GATE / Higher Studies track already defined for the Job-Ready Score. For students choosing GATE, an MS, or a research path over direct placement.
roadmaps.forWho: Students preparing for GATE or applying to MS programs instead of, or alongside, campus placement.

nodes.title: Programming fundamentals
nodes.why: GATE's CS paper assumes fluent C-style programming — not the focus of the exam, but a prerequisite for everything that is.

nodes.title: Data structures
nodes.why: Arrays, linked lists, trees and graphs make up a large, reliably-scored section of the GATE CS paper every year.

nodes.title: Algorithm design and analysis
nodes.why: Asymptotic analysis, greedy, divide-and-conquer and DP — the single highest-weightage topic area on the GATE CS syllabus.

nodes.title: Theory of computation
nodes.why: Finite automata, regular languages and Turing machines — abstract, but a fixed, learnable share of every GATE paper.

nodes.title: Operating systems
nodes.why: Processes, scheduling, deadlocks and memory management — asked in both GATE and almost every systems interview.

nodes.title: Computer networks and DBMS
nodes.why: The OSI model and relational algebra round out the core CS theory GATE actually tests, alongside every other technical interview.

nodes.title: Engineering mathematics and aptitude
nodes.why: A fixed, predictable share of GATE marks that is pure practice, not conceptual difficulty — the easiest marks to lock in early.

nodes.title: Full-length timed mock papers
nodes.why: GATE is a 3-hour exam against the clock — practising untimed teaches the syllabus but not the exam itself.

roadmaps.tagline: Design principles, Figma, usability — reading-heavy
roadmaps.summary: No design-judge here, so this is reading and the student's own Figma file, not tracked practice. Not a path to becoming a dedicated designer — for a developer who wants their own frontend work to stop looking like a developer built it.
roadmaps.forWho: Developers who want to ship better-looking, more usable interfaces themselves, not become a dedicated designer. Fully reading-heavy: no tracked nodes on this platform today.

nodes.title: Visual design fundamentals
nodes.why: Contrast, alignment, repetition and proximity — four rules that fix most of what makes a developer-built UI look wrong.

nodes.title: Typography and color
nodes.why: A type scale and a constrained palette, consistently applied, look more deliberate than a dozen font sizes and colours ever will.

nodes.title: Layout and spacing systems
nodes.why: An 8px spacing grid is the single highest-leverage habit for making an interface feel intentional instead of ad hoc.

nodes.title: Figma fundamentals
nodes.why: The industry-standard design tool — enough fluency to receive a handoff, or mock up your own screen before coding it.

nodes.title: Usability principles
nodes.why: Nielsen's heuristics are old, still correct, and the fastest way to catch an unusable flow before a real user does.

nodes.title: User flows and wireframing
nodes.why: Sketching the flow before touching a design tool catches a confusing journey while it is still cheap to fix.

nodes.title: Accessibility for developers
nodes.why: Keyboard navigation and screen-reader support are not optional extras — and are frequently asked about directly in frontend interviews now.

nodes.title: Redesign one real screen, then explain every decision
nodes.why: Pick a genuinely ugly screen — one of your own old projects works well — and redesign it, ready to justify every choice against the principles above.
